newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax deal could boost equity options business.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax deal could boost equity options business.

text.p: The U.S. equity options industry, already running at full tilt, could get a boost from the repeal of the so-called short-short rule, which was part of the tax package signed by President Clinton on Tuesday.
But even so, some see the industry's record volume as a sign the bull market in stocks may be near a turning point.

Under the short-short rule, a mutual fund's gross income would be taxed if more than 30 percent of it came from short- term gains. The rule effectively limited funds' use of options, which are typically short term-oriented instruments.
But the tax package President Clinton signed today repeals the law, opening the door for funds to use options more.

"Many mutual fund managers have been using our products, but many more want to use them," Chicago Board Options Exchange Chairman and Chief Executive Officer William Brodsky said in a telephone interview after attending the tax bill signing ceremony in Washington.
"This gives managers another tool in their arsenal to increase the yield in their portfolio, or increase their ability to protect portfolio gains," he said.
As it is, the industry is running at a record pace, fueled mainly by retail investors trading individual equity options.

According to the Options Industry Council (OIC), preliminary volume in July topped 26 million contracts, which would be a record. In January, a volume record was set when about 23 million contracts changed hands.
Some brokerage firms were expected to post record options revenue in July.
"We're on track right now to put in the best month in the options product area that the firm has ever seen," an options trader at a brokerage firm in Chicago said last week.
"What's kind of exciting is it's really broad based. People we don't normally talk to," he said.
The head of an equity options department at a New York- based U.S. brokerage house said his firm was also on track for a record July.
"It's just phenomenal," he said. "It's just been steady business. New people keep coming in."
Despite the good times, some see the record pace as troubling.
"The amount of paper flow is very, very broad based," said the options trader in Chicago.

"Generally this kind of broad-based participation -- where you get very high volume in dollars and cents, number of trades and number of clients -- is at turning points," he said. "Well I can hardly imagine we're at the bottom end of a bull market."
Michael Schwartz at Oppenheimer & Co agreed, but said one key new factor is outweighing any historical analysis.
"For the first time in decades we have a high savings rate and that money is going into the market" through retirement plans, he said. "Supply and demand is pushing this market and will continue to."
((--Chicago derivatives desk, 312 408 8750))
